Assuming Postgres and a `users` table (no project here to read the real one from). I haven't run this against a database.

```sql
BEGIN;

ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS first_name text,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_name  text;

-- ponytail: naive split on first whitespace ("Mary Ann Smith" -> "Mary" / "Ann Smith");
-- no general rule exists for names, fix outliers by hand.
-- ponytail: single UPDATE locks every row it touches; batch by id range if the table is large.
UPDATE users
SET first_name = substring(full_name from '^\s*(\S+)'),
    last_name  = NULLIF(regexp_replace(full_name, '^\s*\S+\s*|\s+$', '', 'g'), '')
WHERE first_name IS NULL
  AND last_name IS NULL
  AND full_name IS NOT NULL;

COMMIT;

-- check: should return 0 (blank/whitespace-only full_name rows are excluded, they stay NULL)
SELECT count(*) FROM users
WHERE full_name ~ '\S' AND first_name IS NULL;
```

It is safe to run twice because `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op the second time, and the `WHERE ... IS NULL` guard means the backfill only touches rows it hasn't filled. A re-run also won't overwrite names someone edited after the first run.

Single-word names (`"Cher"`) get `first_name = 'Cher'` and `last_name = NULL`.

Skipped: dropping `full_name` and adding `NOT NULL` constraints. Do the drop as a separate migration once the app no longer reads the column, since it is the only step you can't undo.
